Alamance.analysis: UCMR 5 sampling puts Alamance County in exceedance, with PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxS detected across 4 monitored water systems and a combined severity score of 4.25 — near the top of this batch. The contamination traces partly to textile-era industry: NC State researchers found a textile manufacturer's wastewater discharged to Burlington's sewer was loaded with unreported PFAS-precursor nanoparticles, and concentrations at the Burlington plant have since fallen orders of magnitude after the city used its Clean Water Act pretreatment authority. Sludge is a second front — a September 2026 SELC feature documented an Alamance County farm family whose well was declared "not fit to drink" after decades of PFAS-laced sewage sludge spreading across the road, with seven homes on their road now testing positive. At an August 2026 council retreat, Burlington utilities staff warned that PFAS treatment upgrades and plant capacity work will require multi-million-dollar capital investment funded by revenue bonds and rate adjustments, with initial EPA compliance due 2029 (a 2031 extension possible). The July 2026 Army Environmental Command briefing on the Tarheel Army Missile Plant site in Burlington, where residents distrust tap water despite reported safe TCE/PFAS values, rounds out a county where water trust is thin.

Two weeks later, on September 16, Bladen County announced $26.6 million over ten years from the DuPont/Chemours settlement earmarked for water lines, towers, and system expansion — part of the broader $590 million group settlement covering the state and 11 local entities. That money is meant to shift treatment costs from ratepayers to the polluter. With GenX among its detected compounds, Bladen is the archetypal Cape Fear PFAS county.

Farmer Lake, the town's raw-water source, and Milton's request for help covering grant fees. Caswell is a systems-and-source-water story: filtration, lake management, and emergency interconnections.

Hertford.analysis: Hertford County is the cleanest county in this batch — UCMR 5 shows no EPA MCL exceedances, a severity score of 0, and a single tested public water system. Accordingly, 2025–2026 coverage contains zero PFAS stories; Hertford County Rural Water earns an A grade (100/100) on third-party data sites with no violations on record. The county's real water story is capital replacement: the Town of Hertford is working through a $9.9 million water line replacement project — six months in per the March 2026 town newsletter — replacing 16,600 linear feet of 50-plus-year-old pipe with a Division of Water Infrastructure grant from NC DEQ. The May 2026 update reports crews were eight months in, with paving and patching of affected streets underway across Phase II corridors including Pennsylvania Avenue, King Street, and Railroad Avenue. For readers, Hertford is the reference case: a northeastern North Carolina county where the water agenda is aging pipe, not forever chemicals.

Hoke.analysis: Hoke County exceeds EPA PFAS limits at 2 public water systems with a severity score of 3.75 — driven by PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxS — and the numbers are stark: the Hoke Co Regional–Rockfish system tested at 11.8 ppt PFOS (2.94x the limit) and 6.3 ppt PFOA, while the Hoke Co Regional system showed PFOS up to 4.8 ppt plus lithium above the EPA health reference level. Because Hoke sits downstream of Chemours' Fayetteville Works, its treatment outlook is tied to Fayetteville PWC's $133.7 million granular activated carbon filtration project approved in March 2026 — building-sized facilities that will serve parts of Hoke County and target completion in 2029, two years ahead of the EPA's 2031 deadline. In March 2025, NC DEQ expanded Chemours private-well sampling eligibility into Hoke (and Harnett), making roughly 150,000 more residences eligible for free PFAS well testing. Politically, Sen. Danny Britt — who represents Hoke — is a primary sponsor of the 2025 Water Safety Act (SB 666), which carries a $56 million PFAS Mitigation Fund for grants to local water systems. Of the seven counties in this batch, Hoke's 2026 trajectory is the most directly tied to the Chemours settlement and downstream mitigation.

Broom water treatment plant expansion (completion now targeted June 2026) includes PFAS pilot studies, and Black & Veatch's 2024 regionalization analysis put Johnston's long-term PFAS treatment capital costs at roughly $80 million for its county utility alone. Lee's water story in 2026 is about the treatment gap: contamination pressure upstream, and the race to build filtration capacity to match it.

Sources are a mix of Black Creek/Upper Cape Fear aquifer wells and Neuse River treated water via the Neuse Regional Water and Sewer Authority. Statewide, the July 2026 $244 million drinking-water/wastewater funding round held its application training in Kinston, with applications due September 30, 2026 — a door Lenoir utilities could use for treatment upgrades.

Martin.analysis: Martin County exceeds the EPA MCL in 1 tracked water system (severity score 1.2), with PFOS as the compound of concern: the Town of Williamston's UCMR 5 data shows PFOS at a max of 4.8 ppt against the 4 ppt federal limit (latest test March 4, 2024). The Martin County Regional Water and Sewer Authority has acknowledged the problem — a 2024 request for engineering qualifications stated the raw water intake exceeds the PFOS MCL and sought pilot testing of at least two treatment processes for full-scale design. Separate from PFAS, the county is now at the center of a major environmental lawsuit: on September 16, 2026 the United States and North Carolina sued Domtar Paper Company over alleged decades of dioxin, furan, and mercury releases into Welch Creek, the lower Roanoke River, and Albemarle Sound — waters under fish-consumption advisories since 1990–91. A $1.75 million natural-resource-damages settlement is awaiting final approval for wetland and floodplain restoration. Martin County's water profile in 2026 is therefore two-tracked: an active PFAS treatment-design process on drinking water, and legacy industrial contamination dominating the headlines.

Everything in 2025-2026 water coverage is Hurricane Helene recovery: Helene completely destroyed Burnsville's raw water intake, and DEQ has now directed over $17 million in state water infrastructure funding to Burnsville alone, including $13M in DWSRF/CWSRF funds within the July 2026 $1B Helene recovery milestone. A December 2025 award gave Burnsville $8.2M for drinking water supply and distribution plus $4.9M for sewer line work, and Governor Stein signed Senate Bill 257 in 2026 appropriating $700M+ statewide for Helene recovery. Even routine operations make the news - Burnsville rescinded a system pressure (boil-water) advisory on January 25, 2026. Net read: Yancey's water story is resilience construction, and any future PFAS baseline will be built on infrastructure that's still being rebuilt.
